01 / THE IDEA

Similar motion.
Different contact.

Similar wrist trajectories may correspond to approaching an object, establishing contact, or applying force. Vision and motion alone can leave these phases ambiguous.

TacOT matches temporally extended action–contact patterns. Touch supplies interaction semantics, temporal alignment handles speed differences, and soft optimal transport preserves many-to-many supervision.

02 / THE METHOD

Match through touch.
Learn across embodiments.

Human and robot demonstrations are collected independently, without predefined frame-level pairs. Action–tactile DTW guides soft latent alignment, jointly trained with a flow-matching policy.

01 / SENSE

Unify the observations

Dual-view RGB, a 12-DoF hand representation, and 15 fingertip force channels provide a shared observation space.

02 / MATCH

Match action and touch

Separate action and tactile DTW distances are fused to select a preferred human segment for each robot segment.

03 / TRANSFER

Align and learn a policy

Discount transport costs for preferred pairs while retaining soft coupling over all pairs. Flow matching learns to generate action chunks.

TRAIN → DEPLOY

DTW and OT are used only during training. At deployment, current visual, state, and tactile observations generate 64-step action chunks; the first 8 steps execute before replanning.

05 / THE PLATFORM

Different hands.
A shared interaction space.

The human system combines a Manus glove, Vive Tracker, and five three-axis Paxini sensors. The robot uses a UR5 and XHand. Both record dual-view RGB, motion, and fingertip contact forces.

12 HAND DoF15 FORCE CHANNELS2 RGB VIEWS
Scope and current limitations

Evaluation uses a fixed robot embodiment and RGB observations without explicit 3D geometry. OOD tests target configurations present in human demonstrations but absent from robot training, rather than arbitrary unseen environments. Future directions include heterogeneous robots, depth, and multi-view geometric representations.
